event_info.event_description: Analyze for disclosures on global pandemic risks. Look for corporate language discussing widespread impacts like supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, remote work transitions, and fundamental shifts in consumer demand.

holistic_analysis: HSY’s 2023 Form 10-K acknowledges COVID-19 both as a still-relevant external threat and as a recently realised cost/operational shock.  The risk language spans two categories.  First, forward-looking statements warn that another pandemic wave could disrupt manufacturing, supply chains and macro-demand – positioning COVID-19 alongside other systemic shocks.  Second, the filing cites concrete, recent impacts: mandated retail shutdowns in 2020 and higher 2021 insurance costs tied to delayed medical care.  The disclosures remain largely qualitative and unquantified, but they do connect the pandemic to material areas (production ability, revenues, corporate expenses).  Because the filing date (Feb-2023) falls within three years of the pandemic’s declared onset, the Time Decay Principle permits moderately high scores.  However, the absence of fresh 2023 impacts, the presence of mitigation wording, and the generic ‘could’ phrasing temper severity.  Overall, COVID-19 is treated as an ongoing but now better-managed risk, warranting mid-to-upper-medium evidence scores.

evidence_list.snippet: Disruption to our global manufacturing operations or our supply chain could result from, among other factors, the following: • Natural disaster; • Pandemic outbreak of disease (such as the coronavirus disease 2019 (“COVID-19”) global pandemic); • Climate change and severity of extreme weather; • Fire or explosion; • Terrorism or other acts of violence; • Labor strikes or other labor activities; • Unavailability of raw or packaging materials; • Operational and/or financial instability of key suppliers, and other vendors or service providers; and • Suboptimal production planning which could impact our ability to cost-effectively meet product demand.

components.reason: Explicitly lists a pandemic outbreak of disease, naming COVID-19, as a potential cause of manufacturing and supply-chain disruption.
Links the event to possible impairment of ability to produce or deliver finished goods—direct operational impact.
Risk is identified within three years of the event start, satisfying recent-event window.
Company later claims to have precautions and plans in place, partially mitigating severity.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Strong, recent acknowledgement of COVID-19 as a potential supply-chain disruptor, but softened by mention of mitigation strategies.

evidence_list.snippet: Volatility in food and energy costs, sustained global recessions, broad political instability, rising unemployment, pandemic outbreak of disease (such as COVID-19), climate change, weather, natural and other disasters and declines in personal spending could adversely impact our revenues, profitability and financial condition.

components.reason: Names COVID-19 specifically and ties it to adverse impacts on revenue, profitability and financial condition.
Covers multiple dimensions of financial harm, broadening the risk horizon.
Statement is forward-looking and within three-year recent window.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Direct linkage between COVID-19 and enterprise-wide financial harm justifies a solid mid-range score despite the generic, list-style phrasing.

evidence_list.snippet: At the onset of the pandemic, all Hershey’s Chocolate World stores were temporarily closed and subsequently re-opened in July 2020 with increased safety measures.

components.reason: Describes an actual, realised operational shutdown caused by the pandemic.
Demonstrates direct impact on retail operations (store closures).
Event occurred within the recent 0-3 year window relative to filing date.
States that stores have re-opened with safety measures, signalling mitigation and recovery.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: A concrete historical impact elevates severity, but reopening actions provide partial offset.

evidence_list.snippet: Unallocated corporate expense totaled $614.9 million in 2021 as compared to $520.7 million in 2020 primarily driven by higher incentive compensation, higher group insurance costs from COVID-19-related delays in preventive care and incremental investments in capabilities and technology.

components.reason: Identifies COVID-19 as the driver of increased group-insurance costs.
Provides quantified figures for corporate expenses across two years, showing monetary impact.
Reflects an actual, recent (2021) financial consequence of the pandemic.
Impact limited to corporate expense line item rather than core operations; relative materiality lower.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Quantified but narrow cost impact yields a modest score due to lower strategic materiality.
